newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Weak bullion sparks S.Africa gold industry shakeout.
newsitem.headline: Weak bullion sparks S.Africa gold industry shakeout.

text.p: The South African gold mining industry is undergoing a price-driven shakeout that could create share buying opportunities in the short term and benefit the sector in the longer run, analysts told Reuters this week.

Despite sobering June quarterly results, analysts said there was still mileage in the country's diminished gold-mining industry, whose share of total exports has fallen in a decade from around 50 percent to around 20 percent.
Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd, the world's biggest gold producer, reported second quarter profits down two percent on the previous quarter at 220.7 million rand ($48.1 million).
The company warned shareholders that the future of several mines and shafts was under review.

Randgold and Exploration Co Ltd fared less well in the tight conditions, reporting a pre-capex (capital expenditure) cash loss of 40.95 million rand in the June quarter, down from a 54.99 million rand profit in the first quarter of 1997.

South African mining houses said the weak bullion price had hit revenues in the second quarter and analysts said the gold price fall to 12-year lows earlier this month, and its current soft state, would take its toll in the current third quarter.
In early July the gold price fell to around $314 an ounce and gold was last trading in London at $325.85/326.35 an ounce.

Adrian Allardice, a senior portfolio manager for investment institution Old Mutual, said the bullion price plunge would force some mines to improve efficiency or close, leaving the industry leaner and healthier.
Oasis Asset Management managing director Adam Ebrahim said he saw a healthy shakeout as a result of gold's fall.
"The process is efficient in the long run. High prices bring more producers into the market, lower prices force out those who are not viable," he said.
Allardice said Old Mutual held productive investments in mines and mining houses that had restructured their operations to cope with tighter margins and tougher working conditions.
"We've had a big position in the Anglo group's mines and that looks right, but there is a shakeout under way.
"In general the mining companies seem to be doing the right thing. Maybe we should now start looking at mines who are beginning to bite the bullet on restructuring," he said.

Allardice said Old Mutual had not shifted its weightings in response to the price fluctuations, adding: "With the market having moved so sharply, it's a very interesting time to do some share picking. If you ask me are we trading, the answer is yes."

All the portfolio managers interviewed said they were underweight or at market average weightings in gold, which, on July 30, accounted for 3.5 percent of the Johannesburg Stock Exchange's total market capitalisation of 1,151 billion rand.
Investec commodities fund manager Mark Samuelson said he expected that the restructuring forced by the steady decline in prices would breathe new life into the market.
But he said the same pressure was likely to force a handful of marginal operators out of the industry.
"The question we are all asking is whether the gold price has bottomed out. I would be reluctant to call it that way. I don't think it has hit its bottom.

"With continuing speculation about central bank sales, the gold price is going to remain under pressure. I don't see the price recovering to, say, the $380 level in the short term. Not within the next six months," he said.
Old Mutual economist Erika Prinsloo said central banks around the world still held 34,000 tonnes of gold, equivalent to around 14 years of global gold production.
"Gold's misfortunes will not be temporary," she said.
Dawie le Roux, gold analyst for the Sanlam assurance company, said he believed gold had been through its trough and would "drift higher through the rest of the year".
"I'm mildly bullish on gold.... It's difficult to put a price on it, but I would think the $340 level, where it hung around for quite a while, is a target for year-end," he said.
Le Roux said the $314 bottom reached in July had been an over-reaction to the Australian Central Bank's 167-tonne bullion sale and rumours that other central banks planned to sell gold.
"At the moment, though, the pure economics are coming in with gold mines producing at losses and closing down. At current prices, we're going to see a couple of closures," he said.
-- Cape Town newsroom +27 21 252238 ($ = 4.59 South African Rand)
